docs.title: Public Developer API Reference (v1)
docs.text:
This is the read-only public API for olympiad and competition data. It is intended for school websites, dashboards, widgets, and other public-facing integrations.

  • Base URL: https://olympiad-portal-api.azurewebsites.net/public/v1
  • Local dev URL: http://localhost:3000/public/v1
  • Access: GET only
  • Auth: not required
  • CORS: allowed for any browser origin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The public API exposes non-personal data such as: - olympiad listings - round and calendar information - school rankings and aggregate results - released papers and memos

It does not expose: - student names or personal details - individual answers or marks - private organiser data - protected account information

docs.title: Response format
docs.text:
Every response follows this envelope:

{
  "success": true,
  "data": { ... }
}

Errors follow this shape:

{
  "success": false,
  "error": "Human-readable error message"
}

docs.title: Common rules
docs.text:
• Responses are cacheable for a short time: Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
  • Rate limit: 300 requests per 15-minute window per IP
  • If the limit is exceeded, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests
  • Query parameters for listing endpoints:
  • page (default 1)
  • limit (default 20, max 100)
  • search
  • year
  • sort

Paginated responses usually include:

{
  "page": 1,
  "limit": 10,
  "total": 42,
  "totalPages": 5
}

docs.title: 1.1 Overview
docs.text:
The system follows a client-server, three-tier architecture:

  • Presentation tier — a React single-page application
  • Application tier — a Node.js and Express REST API, structured internally as a modular monolith
  • Data tier — a PostgreSQL database hosted on Supabase

The React application is the only client of the Express API; every read and write of application data passes through hand-written Express endpoints.

The one exception is authentication: React calls Supabase Auth directly to sign users in, sign them up, and reset passwords, receiving a JSON Web Token (JWT) in return. Express then verifies that JWT on every protected request.

Express itself never calls Supabase's data API. It connects to the underlying PostgreSQL database directly through Prisma, and to Supabase Storage directly for file operations.

docs.title: 1.2 Backend Module Structure
docs.text:
The Express backend is organised into modules aligned with the project's feature tiers, so that Intermediate and Advanced tier features can be added without restructuring what already exists for the Basic tier.

Module Tier Purpose auth Basic Role verification middleware; validates the JWT issued by Supabase Auth schools Basic School, educator, and entrant registration rounds Basic Round creation and management; the round state machine (open, running, closed) papers Basic Paper and memo upload, archive, and release gating based on round state submissions Basic Result upload, receipt generation, multiple-choice automatic marking scheduling Basic Automated round opening and closing; notification triggers notifications Basic; extended in Intermediate EmailJS integration: receipts in the Basic tier, reminders and follow-ups from the Intermediate tier marking Intermediate Human marking queue, partial credit, moderation, remarks standings Intermediate Per-school and per-entrant results, certificates progression Intermediate Qualifying thresholds and automatic advancement between rounds questionBank Advanced Question variants and difficulty derived from response data appeals Advanced Appeal routing to a reviewer and outcome propagation to standings tenancy Advanced Multiple concurrent olympiads, each on its own schedule

docs.title: 1.3 Database Schema Design Considerations
docs.text:
Several schema decisions were made up front specifically so that later tiers do not require breaking changes:

  • Submission status is stored as a string field rather than a boolean, so values such as pending review, under moderation, and appealed can be introduced later without a migration that breaks existing data.
  • Entrants are linked to rounds through a join table rather than being embedded directly on the round record. This is what allows automatic advancement between rounds to be implemented as a data operation rather than a schema change.
  • Rounds include a nullable time zone field from the outset, even though the Basic tier can assume a single time zone, so the Advanced tier's multi-time-zone requirement doesn't require retrofitting.
  • Papers and memos are kept independent of any future question bank or variant table, so variants can be introduced later without altering the Basic tier's paper model.
  • The roles table reserves marker and reviewer roles from the outset, even though only organiser, educator, and student roles are used in the Basic tier — so the Intermediate tier's marking queue and the Advanced tier's appeals process don't require a schema change to introduce them.

docs.title: 3.1 Runtime and Framework — Node.js and Express
docs.text: The backend is built on Node.js with Express. This shares a language with the frontend, reducing context-switching across the group, and Express is minimally opinionated — allowing the backend to be organised into the module structure set out in Architecture §1.2 rather than one imposed by the framework. Express also integrates directly with the Node.js job-scheduling libraries the round lifecycle requires.

docs.title: 3.2 API Style — REST
docs.text: The API is a hand-written REST API, documented with OpenAPI. This satisfies the requirement that the API be designed and implemented by the group rather than generated, and is the most straightforward style to reason about across a group with a range of prior experience.

docs.title: 3.3 Object-Relational Mapping — Prisma
docs.text: Prisma is used as the ORM layer between Express and PostgreSQL. It provides type safety consistent with a TypeScript backend, together with a migration workflow suited to a group of six making frequent schema changes early in the project.

docs.title: Olympiad Portal — Bug Tracking
docs.text:
This log records the bugs found in the Olympiad Portal and how each one was fixed. Bugs were found through automated testing (unit, integration and API tests), during deployment, and through use of the portal.

Every bug fixed in the application code has an automated test that reproduces it, so it cannot return unnoticed. See the test policy.

docs.title: Security and data protection
docs.text: ID Area Priority Found by Bug Fix Status BUG-001 Marking Critical API tests Any organiser, or an educator from any school, could change the marks on any answer in any round. The endpoint checked the user's role but not whether they owned the round or the learner. Marking checks that the user is the organiser who owns the round, or an educator marking a learner from their own school. An answer from a different round is reported as not found. Fixed BUG-002 Invitations Critical API tests An educator who had been removed from their school could still create student invitation codes. Creating student codes needs an active school membership, the same as every other invitation endpoint. Fixed BUG-003 Invitations High API tests The public endpoints for checking invitation codes and registering had no limit on repeated requests, so short invitation codes could be guessed by trying many in a row. Rate limiting added to the public authentication endpoints: 100 requests per 15 minutes per IP address, adjustable with AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX. The app trusts the hosting proxy, so each user is counted by their own address. Fixed BUG-004 Error handling High API tests An ID that wasn't a valid UUID (for example /olympiads/abc) caused a server error (500) whose message exposed internal database details and server file paths. Invalid IDs return 400 "Invalid ID format" with no internal details. Fixed BUG-005 Student papers High Use of the portal The student "Download paper" button opened the paper's raw storage path, which doesn't work for private files and exposed where files are stored. A student endpoint returns a short-lived signed download link for rounds the student is registered for, once the round has opened. Storage paths are no longer sent to students. Fixed BUG-006 Invitations Low API tests Invitation responses included the stored hash of the invitation link's secret token. The token hash is removed from responses. Fixed BUG-007 Logout High Use of the portal "Log out" only returned to the login page. The login token, cached student profile and cached data stayed in the browser, so the next person on a shared computer could see the previous user's name and data. Logging out clears the login token, the cached profile, cached page data and saved exam progress, and ends the Supabase session. Fixed

docs.title: Authentication and registration
docs.text: ID Area Priority Found by Bug Fix Status BUG-008 Sign-up Critical API tests Sign-up rewrote some email addresses. For example, first.last+olympiad@gmail.com was saved as firstlast@gmail.com, so the user could not log in with the address they typed. The same rewriting stopped invitations matching the invited address. The email check only trims spaces and converts to lowercase; the address is otherwise kept exactly as typed. Fixed

docs.title: Exams and exam sitting
docs.text: ID Area Priority Found by Bug Fix Status BUG-009 Exam sitting Critical Integration tests Answers could be lost. Autosave used one shared timer, so answering the next question within 0.8 seconds cancelled the save of the previous answer. That answer was also not marked as unsaved, so refreshing the page lost it. Each question has its own save timer. Answers are marked as unsaved until the server confirms them, so they are restored from the device after a refresh. Fixed BUG-010 Exam sitting Critical Integration tests A student who had started but not submitted an online exam was shown as "submitted" on their dashboard and round page, with no way to return to the exam. An online exam that has been started but not submitted no longer counts as submitted, so "Sit exam online" stays available to resume it. Fixed BUG-011 Exam sitting Medium Integration tests The exam timer showed "NaN:NaN:NaN" for a moment while the exam loaded. The timer stays blank until the exam's closing time is known. Fixed BUG-012 Exam sitting High API tests A learner could end up with two sets of results for one round: one captured on paper by their school and one from sitting the exam online. A learner with an online sitting can't also be captured offline, and a learner whose results were captured on paper can't start the online exam (409 in both cases). Fixed BUG-013 Marking Medium Unit tests Selecting the same multiple-choice option more than once could count it more than once when scoring. Duplicate selections are ignored when scoring. Fixed BUG-014 Question builder High Unit tests When a multiple-choice option was left blank, the options after it shifted up on save, but the answer key did not. The saved correct answer then pointed at the wrong option. The correct-answer positions are renumbered to skip blank options before saving. Fixed BUG-015 Exam totals High Integration tests Exam point totals on the exam builder and exam review pages were joined as text instead of added, for example "2" + "3" showed as "23". The database sends points as text. Points are converted to numbers before they are added. Fixed BUG-016 Exam display Low Integration tests A question worth one point showed "1 pts". Points are converted to numbers before choosing "pt" or "pts". Fixed BUG-017 Question builder Medium Integration tests Editing a question and saving without changing its points sent the points to the server as text. Points are sent as a number. Fixed BUG-018 Question builder Medium Integration tests The points and negative marking fields couldn't be cleared: clearing them put the value straight back, so typing "4" produced "14". The fields can be emptied while typing. An empty field returns to its default when the user leaves it, and invalid values show a message and disable saving. The same fix was applied to the marking queue's points field. Fixed BUG-019 Questions Low API tests Questions could be edited or deleted through the address of a different round than the one they belong to. A question that doesn't belong to the round in the address is reported as not found. Fixed BUG-020 Paper viewer High Unit tests The side-by-side paper and memo viewer crashed with "is not a function", because a shared access-check function it used was never exported. The function is exported, with a test confirming it stays available. Fixed

docs.title: Submissions, results and registration
docs.text: ID Area Priority Found by Bug Fix Status BUG-021 Offline results High API tests After submitting results for one learner, the round page hid the submission form, so an educator could only submit results for one learner per round. The round page lists every submission for the school's learners in that round. The form stays open, only offers learners who don't have results yet, and shows a message once everyone is done. Fixed BUG-022 Offline results High API tests The same learner's results could be submitted twice by leaving out the route field on one request and including it on another. The default route is applied before checking for duplicates, so both requests are recognised as the same submission. Fixed BUG-023 Offline results High API tests Results could be submitted for a learner who wasn't registered for the round. Results can only be submitted for learners registered for the round (403 otherwise). Fixed BUG-024 Offline results Medium API tests A submission with no answers was reported as "auto-marked", so the educator's receipt showed "(auto-marked)" even though nothing was marked. A submission with no answers is not reported as auto-marked. Fixed BUG-025 Submissions Low API tests A submission could be viewed through the address of a different round than the one it belongs to. A submission that doesn't belong to the round in the address is reported as not found. Fixed BUG-026 Learner registration High API tests Learners could be registered for rounds that had already closed, been marked or released their results. Registration is only accepted while a round is scheduled or open. Registering for a whole olympiad skips closed rounds, and returns an error if every round has closed. The Entrants page shows which rounds the learner was registered for. Fixed BUG-027 Learner registration Medium API tests The list of registered learners for a round returned an empty list for a round that didn't exist, or for a school not taking part, instead of an error. The list returns 404 for an unknown round and 403 for a school not registered for the olympiad, like the other educator endpoints. Fixed BUG-028 Results Medium Integration and API tests The educator round page showed results as available, and requested them, while the round was still being marked; the server rejects that request. Results are shown as available, and requested, only after they are released. Fixed

docs.title: Reporting a new bug
docs.text:
New bugs are logged as issues in the project's Gitea repository, using the user feedback process. Include:

  1. Role (organiser, educator or student) and the page or endpoint
  2. Steps to reproduce the bug
  3. Expected result and actual result
  4. A screenshot or error message, if available

Once a bug is fixed, with a test that reproduces it, it is added to this log with the next ID.

docs.title: 1. Project Overview
docs.text:
The Olympiad Portal is a web platform that digitises academic olympiad competitions between schools. It replaces paper-based administration with role-based dashboards for organisers, educators, and students.

Problem: Olympiad administration relies on printing papers, manual distribution, physical answer collection, hand-marking, and compiling results in spreadsheets. This is slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale.

Scope: Three role-based dashboards covering olympiad creation, school registration, paper distribution, result submission, automated marking, and results release.

Out of scope: Payment processing, video proctoring, native mobile apps, OMR scanning, multi-language support.

docs.title: 4.1 Database — Supabase (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
The database is PostgreSQL, hosted on Supabase. The data involved is relational in a substantive way — schools, educators, entrants, rounds, submissions, and marks, with constraints such as one submission per entrant per round — and a relational database enforces this correctness rather than leaving it to application code.

Supabase is used strictly as managed infrastructure: Express connects to the underlying PostgreSQL instance directly through Prisma, and the React application never queries application data through Supabase's client library.

!!! note "Why this distinction matters" The Project Brief's Key Requirements name Supabase directly as an example of a system that generates API endpoints, which may not be used in place of a hand-written API. Used only as a managed database, authentication provider, and object store — with all application data routed exclusively through the hand-written Express API — this restriction is not expected to apply. The group intends to confirm this interpretation with the course lecturer ahead of Milestone 1.

docs.title: 4.2 Authentication — Supabase Auth
docs.text: Authentication is handled by Supabase Auth. The React application calls it directly for sign up, sign in, and password reset, and receives a JWT, which Express verifies on every protected request. This satisfies the requirement that authentication rely on an established library rather than a system written by the group, and is a separate concern from the data-API restriction described above.

docs.title: 4.3 File Storage — Supabase Storage
docs.text: Papers, memos, and scanned offline submissions are stored as objects in Supabase Storage, accessed from Express using a service role key rather than by direct, unauthenticated client access.

docs.title: 6. External Integration — EmailJS
docs.text:
EmailJS is the external service integration required of the project, tied to the round reminder, follow-up, and results notification features.

Because these notifications must fire automatically when a round opens or closes, independent of any user action in a browser, EmailJS is called from the Express scheduling module using its Node.js SDK and a private key, rather than from the React frontend using its browser SDK.

!!! warning "Configuration notes" - Non-browser API access must be enabled in the EmailJS account's security settings for backend calls to succeed. - The send method is limited to one request per second, so notifications sent to multiple schools at once are queued and sent sequentially rather than issued in a single loop.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Olympiad Portal integrates the Nager.Date API to identify South African public holidays when organisers schedule Olympiad rounds.

The integration helps organisers avoid unintentionally scheduling rounds on public holidays. If a selected date falls on a public holiday, the system displays a warning. Organisers can then change the date or proceed with the original schedule.

docs.title: Where to Find It in the Application
docs.text:
1. Log in to Olympiad Portal as an Organiser.
  2. Navigate to the Organiser Dashboard.
  3. Select Create Round.
  4. Choose an Olympiad and enter the round's opening and closing dates.
  5. If either date falls on a South African public holiday, the system displays a warning identifying the holiday.
  6. The organiser can select Change Dates or Create Anyway.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
To demonstrate the integration, select 16 December 2026 (Day of Reconciliation) as a round opening or closing date.

The system should display a "Public holiday clashes detected" warning, allowing the organiser to reconsider the schedule.

External API: https://date.nager.at

Integration Type: Third-party REST API

docs.title: 2.1 Framework — React
docs.text: The frontend is a React single-page application, built with Vite. React was chosen because the project requires two functionally distinct interfaces — an organiser console and an educator/student portal — both of which are dynamic and stateful, involving round countdowns, live submission status, and marking queues. React's component model divides this work cleanly across a group of six, and its ecosystem provides supporting components (timers, data tables) that these interfaces require.

docs.title: 2.2 State Management — TanStack Query
docs.text: Most of the application's state is server state — round status, submissions, and marks — rather than local UI state. TanStack Query manages this, providing caching and refetching without the extra boilerplate of a general-purpose state management library.

docs.title: 2.3 Routing — React Router
docs.text: React Router provides client-side routing, with routes gated by role so that the organiser console and the educator/student portal can be served from a single application.

docs.title: 10. Project Methodology — Agile
docs.text: The group has adopted an Agile, Scrum-based methodology.

docs.title: Why Agile + Scrum
docs.text:
1. Iterative delivery for a 4-sprint project. Each sprint maps to a rubric assessment point. Time-boxed sprints deliver working increments independently, avoiding a single end-of-project failure.
  2. Evolving requirements. User stories are defined upfront but implementation details become clearer as we build. Agile allows refinement between sprints without re-planning.
  3. Team size fits Scrum. Scrum recommends 3–9 developers. Our 6-person team parallelises work across three dashboard streams while maintaining direct communication.
  4. Pragmatic ceremonies. Monday/Wednesday/Friday meetings replace daily stand-ups (impractical for a student team with other courses) while providing structured touchpoints.
  5. Trello as product backlog. Columns for Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done. The team collectively prioritises items before each sprint.
  6. Retrospectives drive improvement. Friday reviews include what went well, what did not, and what to change — feeding into the next sprint.

docs.text: This document covers how to execute functional and performance tests on the Olympiad Portal using the standardized Postman collection and environment configurations.

docs.title: 1. Test Artifacts
docs.text:
The Postman artifacts are located in the postman/ directory:

  • OlympiadPortal.postman_collection.json: Standard Postman Collection (v2.1 format) covering:
  • 01 Availability & Health: Liveness probes (/health, /), cold start benchmarks, and uptime verifications.
  • 02 Public API (Performance Archetypes): Unauthenticated public developer endpoints (/public/v1/stats, /public/v1/olympiads, /public/v1/schools, /public/v1/schools/top, /public/v1/activity, /public/v1/calendar, /public/v1/papers).
  • 03 Security & Auth Guards: Verifies that protected routes (/me, /olympiads) reject unauthenticated callers with clean 401 Unauthorized responses without crashing.

docs.title: Option A: In the Postman Desktop App (GUI & Performance Graphs)
docs.text:
1. Open Postman.
  2. Click File → Import (or click the Import button in the top left).
  3. Select postman/OlympiadPortal.postman_collection.json and postman/OlympiadPortal.postman_environment.json.
  4. In the environment dropdown (top right), select Olympiad Portal — Production (Azure).
  5. To run functional test suites:
  6. Click Olympiad Portal — Official API Collection → Run → Run Olympiad Portal.
  7. To run live performance / load tests:
  8. In the Collection Runner, switch to the Performance tab.
  9. Set Virtual Users (e.g. 20 to 50) and Duration (e.g. 1 min).
  10. Choose a load profile (Ramp up or Fixed).
  11. Click Run to watch the real-time latency and throughput curves.

docs.text:
Run directly from your terminal in the root repository directory:

# Run against the deployed Azure production API
postman collection run postman/OlympiadPortal.postman_collection.json

# Run against a local development server
postman collection run postman/OlympiadPortal.postman_collection.json --env-var "baseUrl=http://localhost:3000"

docs.title: Option C: Automated Terminal Load Benchmark (npm run test:perf)
docs.text:
For a direct, high-concurrency throughput and latency percentile breakdown (Avg, p50, p95, p99, RPS, error rates) without needing Postman:

cd backend
npm run test:perf

This runs a native benchmark against all core API archetypes and produces formatted summary tables detailing cold-start latency, throughput, and error rates.

docs.title: Option D: Stress & Crash Resilience Suite (npm run test:stress)
docs.text:
To test the rubric criterion "How often does it crash?" against malformed inputs, SQL injection strings, JSON bombs, prototype pollution, oversized payloads, and high-concurrency bursts:

cd backend
npm run test:stress

This runs a comprehensive 10-vector resilience battery against the live deployment and performs a post-stress health verification probe to confirm zero process crashes.

docs.title: 5. Scheduling
docs.text:
The round lifecycle — a round opening and closing without any manual action — is scheduled using node-cron, running inside the Express process and checking round times at a fixed interval. This requires no additional infrastructure, which is appropriate for the Basic tier's scope.

The scheduling logic is isolated in its own module so that it can later be replaced with BullMQ and Redis, which fire jobs at an exact scheduled time rather than on a polling interval, once the Advanced tier's requirement for a single authoritative clock and exactly-once submission handling under load is taken on. Isolating the scheduling mechanism behind this module boundary means that change will not affect the rest of the codebase.

docs.title: System Design — Olympiad Portal
docs.text: Team: Prompt Engineers Version: v4.0.0 Last updated: October 2026

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
The Olympiad Portal uses a multi-tier architecture with three tiers deployed on separate managed services:

CLIENT TIER                    APPLICATION TIER               DATA TIER
React SPA (Azure Storage) --->  Express API (Azure)   --->   PostgreSQL (Supabase)
Role-based dashboards          Routes > Controllers          Prisma ORM
React Router, React Query      > Services > Prisma           Supabase Auth
                               Helmet, CORS, WebSocket       Supabase Storage

docs.title: Why Multi-Tier
docs.text:
• Separation of concerns: Each tier handles one responsibility (presentation, business logic, data storage)
  • Independent scaling: The frontend is static files served straight from Azure Storage; the backend scales on its Azure App Service plan; the database scales vertically on Supabase
  • Security boundaries: The client never accesses the database directly; all data flows through the API tier which enforces authentication and authorisation

docs.title: Request Lifecycle
docs.text:
HTTP Request
  > Helmet (security headers)
  > CORS (origin validation)
  > Body parsing (JSON / URL-encoded)
  > Route matching
  > requireAuth middleware (validates Supabase JWT)
  > requireRole middleware (checks role: organiser/educator/student)
  > express-validator middleware (validates request body/params)
  > Controller (HTTP concerns)
  > Service (business logic)
  > Prisma ORM (database queries)
  > JSON Response
  > errorHandler (catches all errors, maps to HTTP status codes)

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Custom error hierarchy maps to HTTP status codes:

Error Class Status Use case BadRequest 400 Invalid input Unauthorized 401 Missing or expired JWT Forbidden 403 Insufficient role NotFound 404 Resource does not exist Conflict 409 Unique constraint violation (Prisma P2002) ValidationError 422 Failed express-validator rules

All errors return { success: false, error: "message" }. Stack traces are suppressed in production.

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
• UUIDs for all primary keys — prevents enumeration, safe in URLs
  • Soft delete on users (deleted_at column) — preserves referential integrity
  • timestamptz(6) on all timestamps — timezone-aware precision for deadlines
  • Composite unique constraints — submissions(round_id, entrant_id, route) prevents duplicates; entrant_registrations(entrant_id, round_id) prevents double registration
  • Indexes — rounds(state, opens_at, closes_at) for lifecycle queries; results(round_id, rank) for leaderboards
  • Idempotency key on submissions — prevents double-submission on network retries

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
Registration is open to everyone: invitations are optional for educators and students. School access is either approved manually or granted by an authorised email-bound signup code.

  1. Sign-up: POST /auth/register with a role of educator or student (organisers are provisioned by the administrator). It creates the Supabase Auth user and the users row, plus an educators row and school membership for an educator, or an entrant row for a student.
  2. Choosing a school: educators and students pick from GET /schools. An educator whose school is not listed may name a new one. A student must pick an existing school.
  3. Approval (no invitation code): a new educator's membership is pending. An organiser approves the first coordinator of a school; that coordinator approves later educators and all students. Until then the person can log in but only sees a "waiting for approval" page.
  4. Invitation code (educators or students): an organiser can invite an educator at a selected school, including a first coordinator. An active school educator (coordinator or ordinary educator) can invite educators and students to their own school using POST /school-invitations. A recipient signs up with the emailed address, matching account type and one-use code, gaining active school access without waiting. Student invitations create a new entrant only, never link an existing record by name. Codes expire after 7 days and only hashes are stored. A bad code is rejected rather than falling back to approval. EmailJS delivers the invitation, and the signup link uses FRONTEND_URL.
  5. Joining an olympiad (organiser to educator): the organiser sends an in-app invitation to an educator. It appears on the educator's dashboard; accepting registers their school for the olympiad.
  6. Joining an olympiad (educator to student): the educator invites a student of their own school. Accepting enters that student into every round still taking registrations.

All API requests include Authorization: Bearer <access_token>. The requireAuth middleware validates the JWT via Supabase. The requireRole middleware checks user.role.

docs.title: Round Lifecycle State Machine
docs.text:
scheduled  >  open  >  closed  >  marking  >  results_released
  • scheduled: Round created, opens_at is in the future. No access to papers.
  • open: opens_at reached. Papers downloadable, submissions accepted, online sitting available.
  • closed: closes_at reached. No more submissions. Papers locked.
  • marking: Organiser triggers auto-mark. MCQ scored automatically; non-MCQ queued for human marking.
  • results_released: Scores visible. Papers auto-archived. Qualified entrants identified.

Transitions from scheduled to open and open to closed are automatic, driven by a lifecycle service that queries rounds where the current time has passed the configured threshold.

docs.title: Auto-Marking Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Fetch all submissions with status=received for the round
  2. For each submission, iterate over answers
  3. MCQ answers: compare answer_value to correct_option, award max_points or 0
  4. Non-MCQ answers: set submission status to queued_for_marking for human review
  5. Update submission status to automarked or queued_for_marking

docs.title: Submission Idempotency
docs.text: The composite unique constraint on (round_id, entrant_id, route) plus a unique idempotency_key ensures each submission is counted exactly once, even if the request is retried due to network issues.

docs.title: 5. Security
docs.text: Area Implementation Passwords Min 8 chars, uppercase letter, number required JWT Managed by Supabase Auth; access tokens expire after 1 hour HTTP headers Helmet sets CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options CORS Restricted to one origin in production: the Azure Storage site Input validation express-validator on all routes with sanitisation SQL injection Prevented by Prisma parameterised queries File upload Multer with size limits; PDF only for papers/memos Enumeration UUIDs prevent sequential ID guessing Access control requireRole on every protected route Time-gating Papers locked before opens_at; submissions blocked after closes_at Results embargo Scores only visible when round state is results_released

docs.title: Online Paper Sitting (Sprint 2)
docs.text:
Students sit papers in the browser with a server-authoritative timer. The remaining time is calculated from round.closes_at minus submission.received_at on the server, not a client-side countdown. This prevents timer manipulation via page refresh.

Answers are auto-saved on each change via debounced PATCH requests. On reconnection after a dropped connection, the frontend fetches the submission, pre-fills saved answers, and resumes the server-calculated timer.

The interface includes a question navigator showing answered, unanswered, and flagged questions, with Previous/Next navigation and a flag-for-review toggle.

docs.title: Notification System (Sprint 2)
docs.text:
Organisers configure notification rules with three components: trigger (e.g., "round opens in 24h"), recipient (e.g., "all registered educators"), and channel (email). A scheduler checks upcoming events against configured rules and dispatches notifications.

Rules can be dry-run tested against a past round before activation.

docs.title: Human Marking Queue (Sprint 2-3)
docs.text: Non-MCQ answers are queued with status=queued_for_marking. Markers see a queue sorted by round and question, award partial credit (0 to max_points), and progress through the queue. Moderators sample a percentage of each marker's work for consistency review.

docs.title: Progression and Standings (Sprint 2-3)
docs.text: After results are generated, entrants whose total_points meet the qualifying_threshold are automatically registered for the next round (no manual re-registration). Standings are published at both individual and school level.

docs.title: Question Bank and Variants (Sprint 3)
docs.text:
A central question repository tagged by subject, difficulty, topic, and type. Papers can be generated from the bank with balanced difficulty. Variants give different entrants different question orders or equivalent questions, and marking uses each entrant's specific variant key.

Question difficulty is derived from actual performance data: difficulty = 1 - (average score / max points).

docs.title: Appeals Pipeline (Sprint 3)
docs.text: Students request a remark, which creates an appeal assigned to a reviewer. If upheld, marks are adjusted, results recalculated, ranks recomputed, and qualification status rechecked automatically.

docs.title: Multi-Olympiad Support (Sprint 3)
docs.text: A single organiser account manages multiple concurrent olympiads, each with its own timezone setting. The authoritative clock for deadline enforcement uses the olympiad's timezone. All olympiads share a single archive of past papers.

docs.title: Online/Offline Hybrid (Sprint 3)
docs.text: The same paper is available both online (browser sitting) and offline (downloaded PDF administered on paper). Offline results are uploaded by the educator. Both routes merge into a single result set per entrant. If an entrant appears via both routes, the system flags it for organiser review.

docs.title: Audit Log and Replay (Sprint 3)
docs.text: Every automatic action (round transitions, auto-marking, progression, notifications) is logged with timestamp, action type, actor, and details. Given a round_id, the full event history can be replayed for dispute investigation.

docs.title: 7. Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
Internet
  |
  +---> Azure Storage static website ---> React SPA (built assets)
  |         olympiadportalfe.z1.web.core.windows.net
  |
  +---> Azure App Service (Linux, Node 22) ---> Express API
            olympiad-portal-api.azurewebsites.net
              |
              +---> Supabase ---> PostgreSQL + Auth + Storage

Everything lives in one resource group, olympiad-portal-rg (South Africa North), alongside the Ubuntu VM that hosts the self-hosted Gitea Actions runner.

Azure Static Web Apps would be the natural home for the frontend, but it is only offered in five regions and the subscription's sys.regionrestriction policy permits five different ones, with no overlap. Storage static website hosting is used instead: the built site is uploaded to the $web container, and the error document is set to index.html so unmatched paths fall back to the SPA and React Router can resolve them. The one compromise is that those fallback responses carry a 404 status even though the correct page renders.

Configuration is held where it is used, not duplicated:

  • Backend (App Service settings): NODE_ENV, DATABASE_URL, DIRECT_URL, SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY, FRONTEND_URL, SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT
  • Frontend (baked in at build time by Vite): VITE_API_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_URL, VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY

FRONTEND_URL must match the storage site's URL exactly, since production CORS admits that single origin and nothing else.

docs.title: Olympiad Portal — Testing Documentation
docs.text:
This document covers how the Olympiad Portal is tested:

  1. Testing approach
  2. Automated testing procedure — every type of test, why it is used, what it covers
  3. Running the tests
  4. How CI enforces the tests
  5. Test policy
  6. User feedback process

Bugs found by testing and by users are recorded in bug-tracking.md.

docs.title: 1. Testing approach
docs.text:
The portal has a React frontend and an Express + PostgreSQL backend, used by three roles: organisers, educators and students. Tests are written at four levels, each answering a different question.

Level Question it answers Tests Speed Unit Does each function, component and hook work on its own? 923 Seconds Integration Do the parts work together — services with a real database, whole pages with the app's real logic? 234 Seconds API Does every endpoint return the right response, and let in only the right people? 482 ~45s End-to-end Can each role finish their real tasks in a real browser? 15 ~40s Total 1,654

Most tests sit at the lower levels, because they are fast and point straight at the cause of a failure. A small number of end-to-end tests cover the critical journeys from start to finish.

Suite Location Tools Backend unit backend/tests/unit Jest Backend integration backend/tests/integration Jest + PGlite Backend API backend/tests/api Jest + Supertest + PGlite Frontend unit frontend/tests/unit Vitest + React Testing Library Frontend integration frontend/tests/integration Vitest + React Testing Library + MSW End-to-end frontend/e2e Playwright

Coverage of the backend and frontend source, measured on 29 September 2026 (see Running the tests to measure it yourself):

Suite Statements Branches Functions Lines Backend unit 88.8% 79.2% 87.5% 90.0% Backend API 80.9% 65.3% 77.5% 82.8% Backend integration 67.3% 53.0% 64.9% 70.4% Frontend unit and integration (all source files) 77.4% 68.9% 76.2% 78.4%

The least covered frontend files are the newest pages, which have no tests yet: the organiser's Remarks, Standings, Round replay and Edit olympiad pages, and the educator's Remarks page.

No suite needs a database, a .env file or an internet connection. Everything runs after npm install (plus one browser download for the end-to-end tests).

docs.title: 2.1 Tools, and why they were chosen
docs.text: Tool Used for Why Jest Backend tests The standard Node.js test runner: mocking, coverage and parallel runs built in. Vitest Frontend tests Built for Vite, which the frontend already uses, so tests share the app's build setup. Its API matches Jest's, so one style covers the project. React Testing Library Frontend tests Tests use a page the way a person does — finding buttons by their label, typing, clicking — so they keep working when the code behind them is reorganised. MSW Frontend integration tests Intercepts network calls and answers with realistic backend responses, so pages run their real logic without a server. PGlite Backend integration, API and E2E tests Real PostgreSQL running inside the test process: genuine constraints and data types, with nothing to install. Supertest Backend API tests Sends real HTTP requests to the Express app and checks status codes, headers and bodies. Playwright End-to-end tests Drives real browsers from one install, runs headless without a display, and saves screenshots and traces when something fails. Postman API & load performance testing Standardized collection for live API functional validation, cold-start probing, and concurrency benchmarking (see postman-testing.md).

docs.title: 2.2 Unit tests
docs.text:
What: one function, component or hook at a time, with everything around it replaced by a mock.

Why: they run in seconds, so they can be run on every change, and a failure points at one exact place. They also make it practical to cover every branch — each validation rule, each error path.

Backend — services (auth and invitations, olympiads, rounds, questions, papers, submissions, marking, results, lifecycle, schools, notification rules, educator and student views), controllers, middleware (authentication, roles, validation, error handling, rate limiting), the scheduled round-lifecycle job and helpers. The database client is replaced by a mock, so each test decides what the database returns and checks what the code asked for.

Frontend — UI components, the API client, the Supabase client, login/logout helpers, data-fetching hooks, and the building blocks of each page (question form and cards, marking card, answer-key editor, invitation inbox and invite form, round status labels, dashboard helpers, exam timer, exam storage).

docs.title: 2.3 Integration tests
docs.text:
What: several real parts working together.

Why: unit tests mock everything around the code, so they can't catch problems in the joins — a database constraint, a transaction, a page reading a field the API doesn't send, a number arriving as text.

Backend — real services and Prisma against a real PostgreSQL database:

  1. At the start of a run, an in-memory PostgreSQL database is created and every migration in prisma/migrations is applied in order. This also proves the migrations build a working database from scratch.
  2. The app connects through its normal database code; only the connection address changes.
  3. Every setting is given a safe test value before the app loads, so a developer's real .env can never be used.
  4. Every table is emptied before each test, and the reset refuses to run against anything but the local test database.
  5. Test data is built with shared factories (organisers, schools, educators, rounds, papers, learners, olympiad invitations).
  6. Supabase and email are replaced by fakes.

Covered: the database schema itself, open sign-up in all three roles and the invitation chain (organiser → educator → student), olympiads and rounds, exam building and approval, the online exam, offline submissions and marking, results, educator and student views, schools, notification rules and papers.

Frontend — whole pages inside the real app, with its real routes, API client and data fetching; only the network is faked. MSW answers with the backend's exact response format and records every request, so tests can check what was sent. Any request without a prepared answer fails the test.

Covered: login and sign-up, password reset, account deletion, organiser dashboard and management pages, announcements and archive, exam review and marking, the exam builder, educator pages, student pages, and the full exam-sitting page (timer, autosave, offline saving, submission).

docs.title: 2.4 API tests
docs.text:
What: real HTTP requests through the whole backend — routing, security middleware, validation, business logic, database — checking the real response.

Why: the frontend depends on the API behaving exactly as documented, and these rules protect exam papers, answer keys, marks and learner data.

Complete coverage is enforced. All 110 endpoints are listed in backend/tests/api/helpers/endpoints.js with the roles allowed to call each. From that list the tests automatically check:

  1. the list matches the route files — a new endpoint that isn't listed fails the run;
  2. every protected endpoint returns 401 without a token;
  3. every protected endpoint returns 403 for each role not allowed;
  4. public endpoints work without a token.

Each area then covers the normal case, ownership (users from another olympiad or school are refused), validation (422 with a clear message) and edge cases (a round that isn't open, a duplicate submission, a file over the size limit).

Public developer API. backend/tests/api/public.test.js checks what other websites rely on (any origin may call /public/v1 from the browser while the rest of the API still refuses it, responses may be cached for a minute, and each client's rate limit is reported in the standard headers), every public endpoint's data against a known set of olympiads, schools and results, validation and 404s, paper downloads, and that no response anywhere in /public/v1 contains a learner's name, email, id or own result.

Peak load (A1). backend/tests/api/peakLoad.test.js piles many things onto the same instant and then checks the outcome exactly, not just that nothing failed:

Scenario What must hold 40 rounds due to open or close at the same moment, with three lifecycle ticks running at once Every round opens or closes exactly once, with one audit event each 45 learners around a round's close: some well before, some in its last 150 ms while two ticks close the round, some just after Every deadline ruling matches the moment its request arrived; answers changed before the close count and those after don't; every sitting is marked once, with marks that match the answers stored, and every learner has one result that adds up Ten learners double-clicking Submit Each submission counts once; the second click is told it's already submitted A sitting saved after the close-time marking had run The next tick marks it, so none is left unmarked Three email passes running at once Each educator gets the notice once

Run against the code from before these fixes, three of the five scenarios fail. What was fixed:

  • A sitting is claimed before it is marked, in the same transaction, by the submit, the close-time marking and the next tick alike, so exactly one of them marks it, using the answers saved before the claim.
  • An autosave holds the sitting while it writes and is refused after the deadline, so no answer changes after it has been marked.
  • A round records when it actually closed (closed_at), so a submission that arrived in time counts even if the round closed while the request was being handled.
  • Every tick picks up sittings left unmarked in rounds that have closed.
  • Each email is claimed before it is sent and released if it fails, and a lifecycle tick that comes due while the previous one is still running is skipped.
  • Transactions wait up to 15 s for a database connection (Prisma's default is 2 s), so a burst at the close queues instead of failing.

The test database is PGlite, a single Postgres session behind a socket server, so the integration and API suites use one pooled connection (DATABASE_POOL_MAX=1, as the end-to-end tests already did). Requests made at the same moment then queue for it, as they do for a busy pool, instead of interleaving inside one session. This proves the rules are applied correctly under concurrency; it is not a measure of throughput, which would need a separate full Postgres.

docs.title: 2.5 End-to-end tests
docs.text:
What: a real browser completing real tasks against the real frontend, the real backend and a real database.

Why: the final check that the whole system works for its users — real login, uploads, navigation and browser behaviour. Kept small, because these are the slowest tests.

How it runs: frontend/e2e/servers.ts starts everything for a run: a PostgreSQL database built from the migrations and seeded with known data, a local stand-in for Supabase (sign-in, password reset, file storage), the real backend, and the frontend built the way it is deployed. Tests then click through the UI — they even sign in by typing into the login form.

Journeys covered (15 tests):

Area Journey Accounts Sign in as each role · wrong password refused · log out · organiser sign-up · student sign-up by picking a school · educator sign-up with a new school · password reset from end to end · account deletion Organiser Create a round and upload its question paper, then open it · invite an educator, whose school then shows as invited Exam workflow The educator builds the exam and submits it for review → the organiser checks it and puts it live Competition A student sits the exam online and submits → the organiser closes the round and releases results → the student sees their score Educator Register a learner and invite a student · a student accepts and gets the olympiad

Deliberately left to the faster suites: every validation message, permission checks for all 110 endpoints, offline exam behaviour, and page-by-page detail.

docs.title: 4. How CI enforces the tests
docs.text:
Everything runs through one Gitea Actions pipeline: .gitea/workflows/ci.yml. Deployment sits in the same file as the tests, because a job can only wait for jobs in the same workflow — that is what makes the deploys run after the checks.

Job Runner Pull request Push to main What it does Backend checks & tests ours Yes Yes Prisma schema check, unit, integration and API tests Frontend checks & tests ours Yes Yes Lint, test type-check, unit and integration tests, production build Work out what changed ours No Yes Decides whether the backend, the frontend or both need deploying Deploy backend ours No Yes, if backend/ changed Builds, migrates the database, then zip-deploys to Azure App Service Deploy frontend ours No Yes, if frontend/ changed Builds the site and uploads it to the Azure Storage $web container

docs.title: Where the jobs run
docs.text:
Every job runs on our own runner, prompt-engineers-runner-1, an Ubuntu VM in Azure registered against this repository. It advertises a single label, prompt-engineers-azure, which the shared runners do not, so a job asking for that label can only land on ours — and, because it advertises nothing else, it is never pulled into another team's ubuntu-latest queue.

The end-to-end suite is not part of CI; run it locally (npm run test:e2e in frontend/) before merging changes to a user journey. Playwright, Chromium, a real backend and a PGlite database together need more memory than the VM has: on the 1 GiB VM the suite took 12–18 minutes and still failed tests on timeouts, while swapping heavily. It then ran on the shared runners, but they queued it behind other teams for so long that it rarely reported, so it was taken out of the pipeline on 28 September 2026. Bigger machines were considered and set aside: a 4 GB Azure VM costs about four times the current one, and Oracle's free Arm machines had no capacity in our region.

Our runner takes one job at a time (capacity: 1), so jobs that once ran side by side now queue. That is the cost of guaranteeing where they run.

Supported Node versions: 22, 24 and 26. Every suite (unit, integration, API and end-to-end) passes on each. Both package.json files declare "node": "^22 || ^24 || ^26", so npm prints an EBADENGINE warning on any other version, such as the short-lived odd releases. CI and App Service use Node 22.

Node 24 once broke one frontend integration test, and the cause is worth knowing. From Node 24, fetch's multipart parser builds each uploaded file with whatever File is global, then asserts it is Node's own File. Under jsdom the global is jsdom's File, so the assertion failed inside the mock server and the paper upload never resolved. readBody in tests/integration/support/network.ts now parses uploads with Node's File briefly put back in place. Browsers and the backend are unaffected; it only ever happened in the test environment.

Rules the pipeline applies:

  • Deploys wait for the checks but don't depend on them. Both deploy jobs start once the backend and frontend checks have finished, pass or fail. A red check on main means the deployed code has a problem that needs fixing promptly; it doesn't hold the deploy back. Pull requests are where failures should be caught, so a pull request with red checks shouldn't be merged.
  • Only what changed is deployed. A frontend-only change doesn't rebuild and redeploy the backend.
  • A newer push replaces a run in progress, except on main, where a deploy is never cancelled half way. A cancelled run deploys nothing.
  • The pipeline can also be started by hand (workflow_dispatch), which runs everything and deploys both sides.

docs.title: When tests must be written
docs.text:
1. New features get tests at the levels that fit: unit tests for new logic, an integration test for new database behaviour or a new page, API tests for new or changed endpoints.
  2. New endpoints must be added to backend/tests/api/helpers/endpoints.js with their allowed roles; the suite fails until they are.
  3. Every bug fix includes a test that fails before the fix and passes after it, and is recorded in bug-tracking.md.
  4. Changes to permissions always include API tests for both the allowed and the refused users.
  5. New critical user journeys get an end-to-end test; smaller details stay with the faster suites.

docs.title: Before code is merged
docs.text:
1. All suites pass, along with lint, the test type-check and the build — CI runs these on every pull request.
  2. No test is skipped, deleted or weakened to make a change pass. If expected behaviour changes, the reason goes in the pull request.
  3. Coverage must not drop noticeably. Target: at least 90% of statements at unit level.
  4. Another team member reviews the change, including its tests.

docs.title: How tests are written
docs.text:
1. Independent: each test creates its own data and never relies on another test. The test database is emptied before each one.
  2. No real external services: Supabase and email are faked; no production data or credentials are ever used.
  3. Behaviour, not internals: frontend tests find elements by role, label or visible text; backend tests check responses and stored data.
  4. Realistic data: mocked responses match the backend's real shapes, and records are built with the shared factories.
  5. Clear names that state the expected behaviour, e.g. "responds 403 to another organiser".
  6. Test code is reviewed and type-checked like application code.

docs.title: When tests fail
docs.text:
1. A failure on main is fixed before anything else is merged.
  2. A test that fails intermittently is investigated, not re-run until it passes.
  3. Anything found during testing is logged in bug-tracking.md.

docs.title: Collecting feedback
docs.text:
1. User testing sessions. Before a release, people from each role work through set tasks ("create a round and upload its paper", "register three learners", "sit the exam and submit"). Observers note where they hesitate, go wrong or ask for help.
  2. Feedback form. Afterwards each participant rates how easy each task was (1–5) and says what was confusing, what went wrong and what they would change.
  3. Ongoing reports. Anyone can report a problem at any time, giving their role, the page, what they did, what they expected and what happened, with a screenshot where possible.

docs.title: Recording and triage
docs.text:
Every piece of feedback becomes an issue in the project's Gitea repository, labelled bug, usability or feature request, and given a priority:

Priority Meaning Example Critical Data lost or exposed, or a core task impossible Exam answers not saved; someone sees data they shouldn't High A core task works but gives wrong or confusing results Wrong totals; an action that looks failed but succeeded Medium Inconvenient, with a workaround An awkward field Low Cosmetic Wording, spacing, pluralisation

Issues are reviewed at the weekly team meeting, assigned and scheduled; critical ones are handled immediately.

docs.title: Acting on feedback
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the problem, and where possible write a test that shows it.
  2. Fix it, with that test and all existing tests passing (see the test policy).
  3. Record it in bug-tracking.md and close the issue with a link to the change.
  4. Confirm the fix with the person who reported it, or in the next user testing session.
  5. Raise recurring themes at the weekly meeting and turn them into design improvements.

docs.title: Third-Party Code Documentation
docs.text: Purpose: Describe the external software and services used by the project, why they were chosen, and where they are used.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This document covers the direct dependencies listed in backend/package.json and frontend/package.json, together with the external services used by the deployed application.

The project uses a hand-written API for its main application features. Supabase provides authentication and file storage, while application data and competition rules are handled through the Express API and Prisma services.

docs.title: Backend integration notes
docs.text:
• Express routes call controllers, and controllers pass application logic to services.
  • Prisma is used to access the data for users, schools, olympiads, rounds, questions, submissions, answers, and results.
  • Supabase Auth handles credentials and token verification. The local users table stores application roles and relationships.
  • Supabase Storage stores paper and memo files. The database stores their object paths rather than the files themselves.
  • Nodemailer sends invitation messages through configured SMTP credentials. In development, the mailer logs invitation details when SMTP is not configured.

docs.title: Frontend integration notes
docs.text:
• frontend/src/lib/api.ts is the HTTP client used by pages and hooks. It attaches the stored Supabase access token to API requests.
  • React Router controls page navigation. Backend middleware checks API authorization; the frontend currently relies on the API for access control.
  • React Query is configured in frontend/src/main.tsx and used by selected educator data hooks. Many pages still use direct API calls.
  • Vite produces the static frontend bundle used by the deployment platform.

docs.title: UI Design — Olympiad Portal
docs.text: Team: Prompt Engineers Version: 1.0 Last updated: September 2026

docs.title: Lovable for UI Prototyping
docs.text:
We used Lovable as our primary UI design tool. Lovable is an AI-powered platform that generates modern, visually polished React interfaces from natural language descriptions.

Why Lovable:

  1. Non-generic, visually appealing output. Unlike traditional wireframing tools that produce flat mockups, Lovable generates production-quality components with proper spacing, typography hierarchy, and colour contrast.

  2. Rapid iteration. Design changes that take hours in Figma are done in minutes by describing the change to Lovable.

  3. Design-to-code. Lovable outputs React/TypeScript components that we adapted into our own component library, eliminating the typical handoff gap between design and development.

  4. Built-in dark mode. Every screen was generated in both light and dark variants.

docs.text: Tool Purpose Lovable UI prototyping and component generation Figma UML diagrams, flowcharts, ERD visualisation Lucide React Icon library (1400+ icons, tree-shakeable, uniform stroke) CSS Custom Properties Design token system with OKLCH colour space

docs.title: Colour Palette (OKLCH Colour Space)
docs.text:
OKLCH provides perceptually uniform colours — colours at the same lightness value appear equally bright, unlike HSL.

Light mode:

Token Value Usage --background 98.5% 0.002 250 Page background --foreground 21% 0.02 255 Primary text --primary 48% 0.13 253 Buttons, links, focus rings (deep blue) --secondary 95.8% 0.006 250 Secondary buttons, tags --muted-foreground 48% 0.02 256 Placeholders, secondary text --destructive 53% 0.2 27 Errors, delete actions (red) --border 90% 0.008 255 Dividers and card borders

Status colours:

Token Value Usage --status-open 50% 0.12 155 Round is open (green) --status-upcoming 55% 0.13 70 Round is scheduled (amber) --status-closed 48% 0.02 256 Round is closed (grey)

Chart colours: Five distinct hues chosen for accessibility (distinguishable under colour blindness): warm orange, teal, blue-grey, yellow-green, lime.

Dark mode: Triggered by a .dark class. Background shifts to 12.9% lightness, primary lightness increases to 65% for visibility, borders become semi-transparent white.

docs.title: Authentication Pages
docs.text:
Login page (/login): Centred card on subtle background. Fields for email, password, and a role selector (Organiser/Educator/Student) as tabbed pills. "Forgot password" link and "Create account" link below the submit button.

Signup page (/signup): Same centred card layout. Fields for full name, email, password (with requirements helper text: min 8 chars, uppercase, number), and invitation code with an inline "Verify code" button that shows the school and olympiad details before confirming registration.

docs.title: Organiser Pages
docs.text:
Dashboard (/organiser): Four stat cards (Total Olympiads, Active Rounds, Registered Schools, Papers Uploaded) followed by a table of active rounds with columns for name, olympiad, state badge, and close date.

Olympiads (/organiser/olympiads): Table listing all olympiads. "Create Olympiad" button opens a modal with name and timezone fields.

Create Round (/organiser/rounds/new): Form with round name, olympiad selector, opens_at and closes_at date-time pickers, optional qualifying threshold, and file upload sections for paper and memo PDFs.

Schools (/organiser/schools): Table of registered schools for the selected olympiad. "Invite School" button opens a form for school name and contact email. Shows invitation status (pending, accepted, expired).

Archive (/organiser/archive): Searchable list of past papers across all olympiads with download links.

docs.title: Educator Pages
docs.text:
Dashboard (/educator): Three stat cards (Entrants, Active Rounds, Results) followed by a table of current rounds with action buttons, and a recent results summary table.

Entrants (/educator/entrants): Table of school entrants with "Add Entrant" form (full name, grade) and bulk actions for round registration. "Generate Student Codes" button for bulk login code creation.

Round Detail (/educator/rounds/:id): Round info header with state badge and dates. Paper download button (when round is open). Submission form as a table of entrants with score inputs.

Results (/educator/results): Filterable table by round showing entrant name, score, rank, and qualified status.

docs.title: Student Pages
docs.text:
Dashboard (/student): Three stat cards (Rounds Entered, Best Score, Overall Rank) followed by a table of rounds with state, score, and rank columns.

Round Detail (/student/rounds/:id): When open: timer bar, question-by-question interface with answer inputs (radio for MCQ, text for short answer), flag-for-review toggle, question navigator, and submit button. When results released: score summary, per-question breakdown, and "Request Remark" button.

Results (/student/results): All personal results across rounds and olympiads with certificate download links for qualified rounds.

docs.title: 5. Key User Flows
docs.text:
Organiser creates a competition: Login > Olympiads > Create Olympiad > Invite School > Create Round > Upload Paper > Wait for auto-open > Mark Submissions > Generate Results > Papers auto-archived.

Educator registers and submits: Receive invitation email > Signup with code > Verify school details > Create account > Add Entrants > Register for round > Download paper (when open) > Upload results > View scores (when released).

Student sits a paper online: Receive code from educator > Signup > See open round > Click round > Timer starts (server-calculated) > Answer questions with auto-save > Flag difficult questions > Submit > View results later > Download certificate if qualified.

docs.title: Olympiad Portal — User Stories by Role
docs.text:
Same stories and IDs as the tier-based backlog, regrouped by who the story is for. Each story keeps its tier tag ([B] Basic, [I] Intermediate, [A] Advanced) so you can still filter by milestone within a role. A few stories are written from "the system's" perspective or belong to a supporting role (marker, moderator, reviewer) — those sit in their own section at the end since they're not user-facing in the same way.

For sprint-by-sprint status tracking of these same stories, see the Roadmap.

docs.title: Setup & round control
docs.text:
• [B] B1 — Create an olympiad and define its rounds, so the competition structure exists before anything else can happen.
  • [B] B2 — Register schools against an olympiad, so only approved schools can participate.
  • [B] B5 — Set an opening and closing time for a round, so it runs on a schedule without manual intervention.
  • [B] B9 — Upload a round's paper (and memo), so it becomes available once the round opens.
  • [B] B10 — Have past papers archived automatically once released, so they're browsable without extra work.
  • [B] B16 — Have a console to set up a round and watch its state live, so I have visibility without digging through logs.

docs.title: Progression, standings & rules
docs.text:
• [I] I9 — Set a qualifying threshold on a round, so only entrants who meet it advance.
  • [I] I14 — Configure which reminders/notifications fire, on what trigger and conditions, and what action follows, so I control comms without needing a developer.
  • [I] I15 — Test a configured rule against a real round before it goes live, so I can catch mistakes before they reach schools.
  • [I] I16 — Have standings published per school and per entrant, so results are comparable at both levels.

docs.title: Advanced controls
docs.text:
• [A] A4 — Have a submission that arrives exactly on the deadline boundary settled consistently and defensibly, so no school can dispute the ruling as arbitrary.
  • [A] A5 — Have papers drawn from a question bank, so I'm not hand-assembling every paper from scratch.
  • [A] A9 — Have a single paper sittable either online or on paper, so schools without reliable internet aren't excluded.
  • [A] A15 — Run several olympiads at once, each on its own schedule and timezone, so the portal can serve more than one competition simultaneously.
  • [A] A16 — Have all olympiads share one archive of past papers, so content isn't duplicated per competition.
  • [A] A17 — Have every automatic action the portal takes logged, so nothing happens invisibly.
  • [A] A18 — Replay a round after the fact, so I can see exactly what the portal did and when, e.g. when investigating a dispute.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: • [P] P4 — Have the portal integrate with an external service (e.g. notifications or OMR scanning), so the portal doesn't have to reinvent solved problems.

docs.title: Registration & access
docs.text:
• [B] B3 — Register my school's educators, so they can act on the school's behalf. (school)
  • [B] B4 — Register the entrants I'm putting forward for a round, so their results can be tracked.
  • [B] B17 — Have a single place to find papers, submit results, and collect results, so I don't need separate tools or a shared folder.

docs.title: Round participation
docs.text:
• [B] B7 — Be prevented from downloading a paper before its round opens, so no one gets early access.
  • [B] B8 — Be prevented from submitting results after a round closes, so the deadline is meaningful.
  • [B] B11 — Download the current round's paper and any released past papers, so I can administer the test at my school.
  • [B] B12 — Upload my school's results within the round's open window, so they count toward my entrants' scores.
  • [B] B13 — Get a receipt confirming exactly what the portal accepted, so I have proof of submission if there's ever a dispute.
  • [B] B15 — See my entrants' scores once the round closes (not before), so results are released fairly to everyone at once. (school)

docs.title: Ongoing engagement
docs.text:
• [I] I11 — Be reminded before a round opens and before it closes, so I don't miss the window.
  • [I] I13 — Be notified when results are out, so I don't have to keep checking. (school)
  • [I] I19 — Have a dashboard of all my entrants and their results, so I can see how my school is doing at a glance. (school)

docs.title: Sitting a paper
docs.text:
• [I] I1 — Sit a paper online instead of on paper, so I don't need a physical copy.
  • [I] I2 — See a visible timer while sitting a paper, so I know how much time I have left.
  • [I] I3 — Have my answers saved as I give them (not only on final submit), so I don't lose work.
  • [I] I4 — Resume a sitting exactly where I left off if I lose connection, so a dropped connection doesn't cost me the attempt.
  • Note: needs a server-side authoritative timer, not a client-side countdown, or a refresh could unfairly "reset" time.

docs.title: Access & results
docs.text:
• [I] I18 — Have my own login to sit papers and see my results, so I don't depend on my educator for access.
  • [I] I17 — Get a certificate if I've earned one, so I have something to show for my result.

docs.title: Recourse
docs.text:
• [I] I8 — Request a remark on my result, so I have recourse if I think a mark is wrong.
  • [A] A12 — Appeal a mark, so I have a formal route to challenge a result I disagree with.

docs.title: SYSTEM / SUPPORTING ROLES (not directly user-facing, but essential to design and assign)
System — round lifecycle & integrity
docs.text:
• [B] B6 — Move a round automatically between states at its configured times, so no one has to press a button.
  • [B] B14 — Mark a multiple-choice submission against its memo immediately on submission, so marking doesn't bottleneck on manual work.
  • [A] A1 — Handle every round-open and round-close event correctly even under peak simultaneous load.
  • [A] A2 — Judge a submission against one authoritative clock, so "on time" means the same thing regardless of timezone.
  • [A] A3 — Count a submission exactly once no matter how many times it's retried.

docs.title: System — progression & automation
docs.text:
• [I] I10 — Carry qualifying entrants into the next round automatically, so the organiser doesn't rebuild entrant lists by hand.
  • [I] I12 — Follow up with schools whose submission hasn't arrived, so late-running schools get a nudge before the deadline.
  • [I] I5 — Queue any non-multiple-choice answer for a human marker, so free-response questions can still be marked.

docs.title: System — question bank & unified routes
docs.text:
• [A] A6 — Give different entrants different variants of a paper, so answer-sharing is harder.
  • [A] A7 — Mark an entrant against the exact variant they sat, not a generic key.
  • [A] A8 — Derive each question's difficulty from how entrants actually answered it.
  • [A] A10 — Merge online and offline results into one result set per entrant.
  • [A] A11 — Detect and reconcile an entrant who appears via both routes, so they're not double-counted.
  • [A] A14 — Carry a successful appeal's outcome through into the standings automatically.

docs.title: Marker / Moderator / Reviewer
docs.text:
• [I] I6 — As a marker, award partial credit on a queued answer, so marking reflects partially-correct work.
  • [I] I7 — As a moderator, review a sample of a marker's marking, so marking stays consistent across markers.
  • [A] A13 — As a reviewer, have an appeal routed to me for a decision, so appeals don't sit unassigned.

docs.title: Platform (any user / the team)
docs.text:
• [P] P1 — Sign up, sign in, reset my password, and delete my account.
  • [P] P2 — Use a responsive, accessible portal on any device.
  • [P] P3 — As a developer, have the API hand-written and documented, so the team fully understands and controls its behaviour.
  • [P] P5 — As a new team member or evaluator, have a public documentation site to understand the system without asking the team directly.

docs.title: 9.1 Branching Strategy
docs.text: The group uses Git-flow: a single main branch that is always deployable, with short-lived feature branches merged in through reviewed pull requests. This is simple enough for a group of six to sustain consistency.
